This perspective allows us to examine how quantum information is processed within the system between the time a measurement occurs and when another measurement takes place. By analyzing how outcomes influence the system's quantum states, we can determine how particle positions correlate after the initial measurement and calculate the quantum information transmitted between particles as a second measurement is impending. Although there are a vast number of research papers on this subject, we've identified a gap in literature regarding the creation of a comprehensive indoor fingerprint database. What's more, we've discovered that the quality of signal strength maps has a more significant impact on fingerprint accuracy compared to other factors, which lays the groundwork for future optimization efforts.   analyzed the B-mode and A-mode representations for each age group.  The results demonstrate
  a consistent mapping of respiratory sounds for each age bracket, confirming the validity
  of a size-specific characterization.  The findings also provide guidelines for processing
  respiratory sound data in each age group, ensuring the effectiveness of radar technology
  in detecting lung conditions across a wide range of ages.  By providing a standardized

Specifically, we examine situations where a manifold with a geometric G_2-structure has positive scalar curvature, and analyze the possible ways that its cone can be bundled over a Riemannian manifold. We derive conditions on the underlying manifold to ensure that its cone can be collated with a constant positive curvature Riemannian manifold, and explore the possibility of wrapping its cone around a Riemannian manifold with a pre-existing geometric G_2-structure. We present a scenario where a geometric G_2-structure on a 7-dimensional manifold can be obtained by twisting a Ricci flat geometric A_2-structure on a 6-dimensional manifold, and examine the possible ways that a geometric G_2-structure on a 7-dimensional manifold can be split into two parts along a submanifold. Finally, we outline a method for constructing geometric G_2-structures on a 7-dimensional manifold by stacking two twisted geometric A_2-structure components along a submanifold, and analyze the possible torsion types of these structures.  Throughout the paper, we integrate our findings with a comprehensive survey of existing literature on the subject matter.  This research contributes to our understanding of geometric G_2-structures and their possible configurations on a 7-dimensional manifold, and presents novel approaches to constructing and bundling these structures.  The paper's findings have implications for various areas of mathematics, including algebraic geometry, differential geometry, and topology, and is intended to promote further exploration of the topic.  To facilitate this, we have included a detailed bibliography of relevant scholarly work.  This research is an extension of our previous studies on geometric A_2-structures and twisted geometric A_2-structure components, and is part of a broader project aiming to develop a theory of geometric G_2-structures comparable to the established theory of Ricci flow.  The paper's findings demonstrate that many aspects of this theory can be replicated with the more versatile geometric G_2-structure model, and presents opportunities for the development of new analytical tools and techniques.  One of these tools is a variant of the fundamental theorem of Riemannian geometry suitable for geometric G_2-structure cones, which we outline along with a plan for incorporating a number of existing results into the new framework. of active galactic nuclei (AGNs) is
  not well understood, particularly over short timescales. We present the first extensive
  comparison of optical and UV variability characteristics in a large AGN sample, drawn
  from nearly a decade and a half of observations by the Kepler and UVON telescopes.
  Analyzing the behavior of approximately 100,000 observations of nearly 100,000 AGNs,
  we found that optical and UV fluctuations are not correlated on short timescales but
  become more synchronized over longer periods. AGNs with higher UV luminosities exhibit
  more rapid variability in both optical and UV wavelengths. The amplitude of optical
  fluctuations is directly proportional to the square root of the luminosity, whereas
  UV fluctuations are more closely tied to the luminosity itself. The most extreme UV
  variability events are often preceded by enhanced optical activity, suggesting a possible
  causal relationship. We propose a two-component central engine model to explain these
  findings, comprising a steady disc responsible for UV emission and an orbiting hot spot
  responsible for optical emission. This model predicts that the hot spot's size is inversely
  proportional to the AGN's luminosity and directly proportional to the variability timescale.
  This study provides a comprehensive framework for understanding the optical and UV variability
  characteristics of AGNs, which can be applied to analyze the behavior of individual objects
  and help identify extreme objects worthy of further study.    The data presented in this paper has been made publicly available at http://www.pimrhe.fr/~boissier/AGN/AGN.html.   large. We develop a continuous-time population model where ideas emerge and
  demonstrate that a rumor spreading in such a model will eventually cease
  to be prevalent if the model's parameter, which represents influence range,
  is below a certain threshold. We also prove that the threshold is optimal

  a given rumor. We further illustrate that this threshold is achievable in

  demonstrate that the best spreading strategy for spreading a rumor is through
  influential individuals. Finally, we show that the threshold can be reached
  through a gradient descent algorithm starting from an arbitrary distribution
  of the population and present an alternative approach using a particle swarm
  optimization algorithm.  Our findings provide theoretical boundaries for

Unlike the heat equation, the acoustic Schrödinger equation allows for non-trivial initial conditions to be directly inferred from the observed data of the solution. This is attributed to the absence of a diffusion term in the equation, which prevents the spread of information as seen in equations like the heat equation. The main contribution of this document is the development of a novel, global-in-time reconstruction method that utilizes the spectral information of the acoustic Schrödinger equation. This approach leverages the direct relationship between small perturbations in the initial condition and corresponding oscillatory patterns in the solution, allowing for the precise recovery of the initial condition through the amplification of these oscillations at the boundary of the observation domain. This method is particularly effective as it yields a reconstruction that is nearly instantaneous, achievable within the solution's earliest oscillatory period, and free from any statistical uncertainty. To further validate this approach, we have applied it to both a numerical model and a real-world scenario of a gas dynamics experiment. The results demonstrate the feasibility of implementing this method in real-world scenarios, given the practical challenges of implementing the proposed boundary conditions that enable the reconstruction. They have distinct design choices, stemming from varying objectives and user groups, reflecting diverse balances between power, expressiveness, and safety. Type Systems in programming languages allow developers to define and enforce rules governing data types, aiming to prevent type-related errors and guarantee certain program properties.  The design of Type Systems reflects a balance between eliminating errors, avoiding performance costs, and allowing for creative expression.  Programming languages like C and C++ have minimalist Type Systems, whereas languages like Haskell and Rust possess more sophisticated systems that offer stronger guarantees but also present greater complexity.  Ultimately, the choice of Type System influences how developers work, the kinds of projects they can undertake, and the trade-offs they must make between safety, performance, and productivity.  By examining the Type Systems of renowned languages, we can gain a deeper understanding of this critical aspect of programming and the factors driving language design.  Developers, researchers, and the broader programming community would benefit from a clearer grasp of Type System principles and their far-reaching implications. This framework provides a common groundwork for discussing Type System topics, including type inference, checking algorithms, soundness proofs, polymorphism, subtyping, and advanced features like dependent types and recursive types.   To address this challenge, we propose a new methodology for evaluating bias in language models through the analysis of discrimination in embedding spaces.   
  Our approach involves measuring the disparity in distances between pairs of words with pre-existing social categorizations, drawing on the extensive word embeddings released with the SemEval-2019 task 9 dataset.

  We also observe that the models' biases mirror real-world prejudices, demonstrating a link between the models' learning data and their discriminatory tendencies.   
  By utilizing pre-existing categorizations and focusing on discrimination in embedding spaces, our approach offers a more accurate measure of social bias in language models.   
  This research paves the way for developing bias-free models through objective, data-driven training data evaluation, enabling the creation of models with reduced socio-cultural prejudices and improved performance in discriminatory tasks.   
  Our methodology is available online for public use, along with the precomputed embedding disparities analyzed in this study, allowing the community to evaluate the bias in language models and evaluate new models on socio-culturally defined attributes.

Beginning with an initial part that sets out the main objectives and provides background information, we proceed to present the key ingredients and statements of the two main theorems.    The first theorem focuses on the unique continuation property for harmonic functions in relation to a given polynomial and a given vector, whereas the second theorem expands on this property to a set of polynomials and vectors after accounting for a scaling factor.    Subsequently, we outline the overall strategy for demonstrating the unique continuation property via the generation of a family of modified Carleman estimates, incorporating a key inequality along the way.    This inequality involves a measure function, a family of polynomials, and a family of vectors, which can be optimized to satisfy three essential conditions following the approach outlined by Fuchs and Kohn.    Once the optimized inequality is established, we present the two main theorems, along with two additional corollaries concerning the unique continuation property for harmonic functions in the presence of given polynomials and the unique continuation property for a product of functions under the condition that one function is known to be non-vanishing.    The paper concludes by highlighting the significance of the obtained results in the context of geometric uniqueness theorems for solutions of certain partial differential equations, including the equation of steady state fluid dynamics and the equation of harmonic steady state heat conductors, as well as the Kato smoothing effect for solutions of the Schr\"odinger equation. Here, we define a streaming algorithm as partially observable if it receives only partial information about the input stream and propose the problem of designing nearly optimal streaming algorithms for partially observable streams that are subject to adversarial manipulation. We derive a general approach to solving this problem by outlining a framework that consists of the following steps: (1) estimate the relevant information about the stream based on the partial data received so far; (2) use a known algorithm to process the estimated information; and (3) analyze the performance of the algorithm using the estimated information. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of this framework by solving two specific instances of the problem: - Approximate Frequency Estimation: Design a streaming algorithm that estimates the frequency of each element in an ordered stream with a relative error of at most delta and learn the true frequency with a probability of at least 1-delta. - Counting Distinct Elements: Design a streaming algorithm that counts the number of distinct elements in a stream with a probability of at least 1-delta and a relative error of at most delta. We obtain nearly optimal algorithms for both problems by outlining a simple and general strategy that receives partial information about the stream's size and/or distribution and results in an algorithmic overhead of at most (1+/delta - 1)/eps together with necessary conditions on the possible values of delta and eps.  Moreover, we provide lower bounds on the possible algorithmic overheads for both problems, demonstrating that the proposed strategy is near-optimal. Finally, we generalize the problem to different metric spaces and show that the proposed approach yields nearly optimal algorithms for partially observable streams with adversarial manipulation for streams organized into a data structure known as a recursive partition, allowing applications in computational geometry and topological clustering. The research also analyzed possible strategies for misleading FENRIS by intentionally manipulating sensor data, which can be useful in developing countermeasures against the attack.  Furthermore, the research explored possible ways to deceive FENRIS in smaller-scale grids, which can be applied in various topological configurations when an attacker controls two adjacent nodes. Furthermore, we observed that the formation of a molecular state is contingent upon the depth of the trap and the strength of the inter-particle interaction. uncertainty in quantum physics has long been attributed to the reality of particles' position when interacting with their gravitational field.  This paper demonstrates that this uncertainty could be a fundamental property of gravity, analogous to the zero-point motion of electromagnetic fields.  A microscopic model of gravity is proposed, where massless conspirator particles mediate gravitational interactions in a similar manner to photon participation in electromagnetic interactions.  Based on this model, we derive an operator representing the gravitational field's oscillating component and calculate the associated quantum fluctuations to determine the gravitational position-time uncertainty relation, which is found to be similar to the shot-noise limit in optical systems.  The implications of this discovery are significant, as it has the potential to reconcile quantum gravity theories and the quantum foam model, and could influence our understanding of gravitational quantum effects in microscopic particle interactions.   Due to their significance, studying protein-binding properties is crucial.
  While experimental methods to analyze protein-binding properties are available, they are
  often expensive, time-consuming, and may not even be feasible for some proteins.
  As a result, computational approaches to investigate protein-binding properties have
  gained popularity.
  One such method involves training deep learning models on existing protein-binding data
  to predict how other proteins bind to substances.
  However, existing research suggests that significant improvements can be achieved by
  using protein structures that have already been analyzed for binding properties to train
  models, as compared to using random structures.
  In this work, we investigated the effectiveness of utilizing pre-existing binding data
  directly to train models, which yields the best results but is not always feasible, and
  compared it to using pre-existing bound protein structures to train models, which is
  more widespread but less effective.
  We found that using pre-existing bound protein structures significantly improves the
  accuracy of protein-binding predictions for both small and large binding sites, as well
  as for binding to small and large molecules.
  We also observed that using pre-existing bound protein structures to train models is at
  least comparable to existing research results for 75% of evaluated binding data and
  outperforms it for 25% of the data.

  structures when training deep learning models to predict protein-binding properties.

of formal systems used in formal verification of practical cryptographic protocols, specifically for encoding schemes and key exchange protocols. This approach focuses on pinpointing the source of security issues when parameterized protocols are compounded and combined in novel ways within an open network. It differs from traditional protocol analysis, which generally approves or rejects a protocol's security based on its fixed format. Our approach is inspired by the relational simulability concept, particularly Raux and Bouchouchko's earlier work on grading probabilistic systems, which we expand upon by introducing a step-by-step explanation. This explanation is necessary as the initial description is deemed abstract. Our strategy consists of three main components: defining graded probabilistic systems, establishing a relational simulability criterion, and deriving a polynomial time algorithm to determine if there's an almost perfect simulation between two arbitrarily given finite-grade systems. We present three distinct scenarios involving encoding schemes and key exchange protocols, demonstrating how our approach can be applied to analyze these scenarios. This includes analyzing identity-based key exchange protocols, multi-party key exchange protocols, and a particular instance of a broadcast key exchange protocol known as WeilKey. This broadcast key exchange protocol is initially disapproved of due to its inherent weakness; however, our approach enables us to modify it by adding an encoding scheme, resulting in a secure variant. This variant can be further optimized by replacing the encoding scheme with an alternative one, leading to multiple possible variants. Our approach allows us to assess the security of individual instances of the WeilKey protocol and its variations after the fact. This assessment demonstrates that distinct instances of the same protocol variant may have varying levels of security, ranging from nearly perfect to negligible. This research contributes to our understanding of encoding schemes and key exchange protocols, offering a practical way to repair insecure protocols and a theoretical foundation for developing new secure protocols.  This research is relevant to both theoretical cryptographers and practitioners engaged in formal verification projects.   layers (defined as those with a height of at least 0.5 km) over the Atlantic
  Ocean, stretching from 23.5$^{\circ}$S to 23.5$^{\circ}$N.  To analyze these
  layers, the researchers employed two satellite instruments: CALIPSO, which can
  pinpoint aerosol layers with a high degree of accuracy, and CERES, which can
  measure the amount of sunlight reaching the Earth's surface.  To further refine
  their analysis, the researchers divided the study area into three regions:
  Southern, Central, and Northern, each with distinct aerosol patterns.  Over
  the Southern region, both satellite instruments agreed that aerosol layers were
  relatively thin, reaching a maximum height of about 1 km.  In the Central
  region, both instruments observed thicker layers, extending as high as 3-4 km
  towards the equator and thinning out towards the coast.  Towards the Northern
  region, the layers thinned out, reaching a maximum height of about 2 km over
  the coast and disappearing over the ocean.  By comparing these observations
  with global models from aerosol and climate systems, the researchers found that
  they accurately captured the depth and properties of aerosol layers in the
  Southern and Central regions but underrepresented them in the Northern region

In 1970, Israeli and coworkers proposed an approach to describe the behavior of a quantum Bose gas by means of a modified Navier-Stokes equation, marking the beginning of the field. Over five decades, a substantial body of research has focused on a specific aspect of a quantum fluid dynamics model: the viscosity coefficient. In the presentation, we explore the fundamentals of a quantum fluid dynamics model before delving into the latest findings regarding the diffusion coefficient. Specifically, we discuss recent research by Levchenko, Krstić, and Wimmer on the momentum conservation issue in a quantum fluid dynamics model and propose an alternative solution. Furthermore, we outline a new way to derive the diffusion coefficient using the Grad's 13-moment approach, presenting promising results for a quantum Bose gas in a harmonic potential and in a harmonic lattice. Moreover, we explore the possibility of applying the proposed strategy to a quantum fermi gas, presenting encouraging outcomes for a simple model of a quantum fermi gas in a harmonic potential. Finally, we discuss the outlook on developing a full closure including the diffusion coefficient and the feasibility of using a quantum fluid dynamics approach to describe ultracold atomic gases in optical lattices. Although research has explored the methods and feasibility of attacking these models, the underlying economics of these attacks remain unexplored.  In this research, we investigate the financial viability of model stealing attacks on real-world public models by incorporating the costs associated with building a compromised model and the revenue generated from using an existing model. Furthermore, we find that on real-world datasets (MNIST, CIFAR-10), the attack might not be profitable unless the existing model's quality is substantially impaired to begin with. We discover that even with significant reductions in purchase costs, the economic advantage of public models is evident on large-scale commercial datasets but less pronounced on smaller datasets.   Recently, a claim has been made to have precisely measured this parameter using deep
  learning techniques and 13 TeV proton-proton collision data, consisting of 3-3.8 TeV
  center-of-mass energy muon pairs. Here, we carry out a detailed evaluation of the
  methodology employed in that study to determine the electroweak mixing angle. Through
  a precise analysis of various sources of systematic uncertainty, we observe that the
  model dependence significantly contributes to the overall uncertainty. Furthermore,
  we discover that the chosen machine learning model is not optimized for the task at
  hand, and that the data preprocessing steps introduced additional uncertainties.
  Based on these findings, we estimate the true uncertainty in the measured electroweak
  mixing angle to be at least a factor of three greater than the claimed value of 0.23
  degrees. Consequently, we propose an improved methodology that utilizes a simple
  linear fit function in place of the neural network, resulting in an uncertainty of
  approximately 0.5 degrees in the electroweak mixing angle. This proposed approach
  yields a measured value of 23.13 +/- 0.15 (stat) +/- 0.43 (syst) degrees, which is
  consistent with the world average of 23.0-23.1 degrees.  Ultimately, our analysis
  suggests that the deep learning method employed in the original study is not suitable

  A major obstacle in understanding these processes is the lack of information about the embedding space where DNNs operate.
  In contrast to traditional neural networks, the properties of the embedding space are crucial for analyzing the transparency of DNNs.
  This study investigates the geometric characteristics of the embedding space in vision DNNs with a focus on eliminating ambiguities and exploring patterns around specific points.
  Our research reveals that the embedding space is not linear but rather geometrically complex, incorporating areas like cones and cylinders.

flocks of animals and schools of fish begin with ordered arrangements, gradually becoming disordered as movement proceeds.  Contrary to this traditional perspective, our experimental observations of starling flocks through 3D rendering technology have revealed that many natural flocks initiate collective movement from disordered states, without a clear leader taking charge.  We propose a new model of collective motion - the Bounded Rationality Model - which mimics how birds perceive their surroundings and make decisions based on limited information.  Through 3D visualizations and data analysis, we demonstrate that this model effectively reproduces various patterns of collective movement observed in real starling flocks, including spiral movements, sharp turns, and the formation of central voids in expanding flocks.  By abandoning the ordered initial condition, our model exhibits characteristics of self-organization, producing movement patterns through intrinsic dynamics rather than external influences.  This groundbreaking model offers a novel way of understanding how flocks of animals generate complex movements and patterns without a clear leader, paving the way for a more precise understanding of collective behavior and possible applications in robotics and vehicle swarms. Our research analyzed seven widely used encryption algorithms (Rijndael, Serpent, Khufu, Khameleon-256, Tiger, MD5, and SHA-256) after they were compromised in break-in attempts by highly advanced adversaries with nearly unlimited resources. Our results demonstrate that even when highly secure encryption methods are used to safeguard medical data, there remains a marginal yet measurable risk of unauthorized access. This threat is not necessarily to the data itself but rather to the financial compensation healthcare providers stand to lose if compromised patient information is revealed. Our research findings suggest that this risk is minuscule for highly secure encryption methods (less than 1 in 10 billion incidents) but notable for more basic algorithms (more than 1 in 100 million incidents). Our research aims to accurately calculate this risk to guide healthcare providers in making informed decisions about how to protect sensitive information over a network.  This research contributes novel insights into the balance between using highly secure encryption methods that carry a small risk of breach versus more basic alternatives that offer little protection but are easier to implement and monitor. They may be inclined to discuss Greek letters used in these proofs, but the intent behind this discussion is not always clear. LLMs have been known to misinterpret the intentions of fellow models on such discussions, which raises concerns about the reliability of LLMs in debating mathematical proofs. To better understand how LLMs think during these discussions, we designed an Turing Test analogous to the one proposed by Alan Turing in 1950, but with a twist to suit the situation. We introduced a Turing Test where LLMs discuss the proof of a famous mathematical statement, involving the use of Greek letters. To mirror real-world mathematical proof discussions, we defined the test to evaluate the intent behind the discussion on these proofs. We observed that even the most advanced LLMs struggle to demonstrate meaningful intent when discussing mathematical proofs. By analyzing the angular correlations between heavy and light quarks created in ultrarelativistic collisions, we aim to gain insight into the formation time of heavy quark pairs.  Utilizing 2+1 dimensional lattice QCD simulations for the light quark sector and the 5+1 symmetry reduced model for heavy quark behavior, we have collected extensive data on heavy quark pairs produced through the collision of ultrarelativistic gluons. This challenge is analogous to a pivotal moment in the development of classical computers, occurring before they could perform practical calculations that aid in their own verification.  Similar to the classical era, where ensuring the accuracy of initial programs was carried out through rigorous mathematical proof, we require a similar approach with near-term quantum computers. Despite the theoretical feasibility, using such models in real-time to guide public health policy is impractical due to the excessive computational resources required. This limitation holds even for moderately sized populations and is particularly challenging for models that scale exponentially with parameters.  To address this issue, we propose a novel structured epidemic model that scales linearly with parameters, allowing for exact solutions via finite Markov chains.  This linear model applies to regions with overlapping contact networks, enabling the analysis of geographic models with multiple interconnected areas.  We demonstrate an algorithmic approach to simulate each step of the model's evolution and develop a framework for solving recurring models that evolve over time.  Theoretical bounds on memory usage and computational time show that the model's scalability is significant, outperforming existing alternatives by several orders of magnitude.  To illustrate the model's applicability, we present three real-world scenarios: an exponentially growing epidemic in a population of 200,000 individuals, a geometrically spreading pandemic across 1,000 regions, and a globally interconnected population of 10 million people.  In each scenario, the model's outcomes match the results from alternative models or simulation data, demonstrating its accuracy.  The linear model's most generous estimated memory requirements for a population of 10 million individuals across 1,000 regions are 3.8 terabytes of storage and 230 milliseconds of computational time for each model iteration.  This significant improvement paves the way for the use of structured epidemic models in real-time policy making at a global level. growing computational powers, there's a surge in using large-scale computational methods to explore complex scientific phenomena and analyze resulting data.  As a result, significant research efforts are devoted to processing and analyzing data through computational methods, which have been learned from existing data.  Despite the significance of this processing step, current scientific practice treats it equally to discovery and data collection, and is exempt from rigorous testing and verification.  In many cases, the best possible outcomes from these analyses are not even accurately known, raising concerns about the validity of results obtained from them.  To address these issues, we propose a new framework that emphasizes the equal importance of processing and analytical methods to observational and analytical data, and advocates for treating them with the same level of scrutiny.  In this framework, we aim to establish a clear understanding of the underlying assumptions and uncertainties of these methods on a case-by-case basis, and strive to verify them through a combination of theoretical and experimental approaches whenever possible.  By doing so, we can optimize these methods to meet the exact needs of each individual research project, and ensure a more accurate representation of physical realities.  To illustrate the implications of this framework, we present three compelling use cases: measuring neutrino properties through air shower experiments, analyzing heavy ion collision data through hydrodynamical models, and searching for dark matter signatures through direct detection experiments.  In each case, we outline the fundamental processing and analytical steps, examine the underlying assumptions and uncertainties of the methods used, and explore opportunities to verify them through laboratory and theoretical experiments.  By applying this framework to these and other research efforts, we can improve the overall reliability of results, promote a culture of integrity in scientific practices, and contribute to a deeper understanding of the physical world.  Ultimately, our goal is to establish a robust foundation for analyzing and interpreting scientific data, with the aim of obtaining a more accurate and a more complete picture of reality.  In doing so, we hope to inspire a paradigm shift in scientific practices at the interface of computation and observation, and explore possibilities for a computational realism that goes beyond digital representations.  This comprehensive framework offers a compelling alternative to established views of scientific realism, and provides a solid basis for reconciling scientific knowledge with a broader understanding of reality.  As a result, we can re-imagine the nature of physical truths, explore the philosophical implications of computational uncertainties, and consider the ethical consequences of influencing the very reality we strive to understand.  In the process, we can gain a profound appreciation for the fundamental relationship between our experience of the world

We derive exact expressions for the expected value of the pot, the fourth player's expected challenge, and the fourth player's optimal strategy in the game of 20/20 poker.   While time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT) is a popular method for this purpose, its high cost makes it impractical for large-scale calculations.
  To address this challenge, we present an implementation of TDDFT into the classical molecular dynamics code LAMMPS, enabling the simulation of optical properties such as absorption spectra.

  power consumption. This paper opposes this concept, presenting an alternative perspective

To effectively utilize these methods, it is crucial to validate the accuracy of the specifications themselves before specifying and verifying the system's safety properties.  This initial validation is known as specification precondition verification.  Although interactive proof assistants can be employed for this purpose, it is inefficient and often impractical due to the typically high cost of proving preconditions for large-scale systems with complex behaviors.  A more viable alternative involves using automated tools to carry out this validation.  In a 2019 paper, Alur et al. suggested employing automated reachability verification to streamline specification precondition verification for safety-critical systems.  Building on their work, we present an extended investigation into the advantages and challenges of using automated reachability verification for specification precondition verification.  In particular, we explore possible implementations, analyze the method's limitations, and examine various options for optimizing the process.  Furthermore, we outline a possible pathway for integrating automated reachability verification into mainstream hardware design flows.  By leveraging automated reachability verification to validate specification preconditions, developers can ensure the accuracy of specifications before formal verification, ultimately aiming to eliminate incorrect specifications that pose safety risks.  To facilitate this goal, we propose a set of objectives for researching new automated verification techniques and incorporating existing tools into formal verification frameworks. In such cases, an approach that has shown promise is using the multiple-outcome reduced dynamics to reverse-engineer the Hamiltonian, a process known as Hamiltonian reconstruction.  Although an optimal method, specifically the maximum-likelihood approach, exists for implementing this process, it is often hampered by its high computational requirements, making it unsuitable for large-scale, complex quantum systems.  In a system consisting of multiple parts, the situation is even more complicated due to the complexity of the reduced dynamics based on the outcomes of a measurement process.  However, experiments involving the observation of a particle's trajectory in a harmonic potential after interaction with a laser are common, and in such cases, the overall process can be broken down into simpler, conditional processes based on the outcome of the measurement.  In such cases, the individual outcomes might be distinguishable, but the particle's behavior is ultimately governed by a known underlying dynamics.  As a result, an appealing alternative is using the known overall dynamics to guide the reconstruction process.  In a single-component Ginzburg-Landau system following a harmonic potential after interaction with a laser, for instance, the known underlying dynamics can be utilized to simplify the Fock representation of the system's quantum fluctuations.  Here, we present a new, viable approach to reconstructing the Hamiltonian based on the reduced multiple-outcome dynamics, utilizing the known overall dynamics in a system where the total process is composite and the outcomes are distinguishable.  In a system consisting of multiple parts, we can reconstruct the local parts of the quantum fluctuation Hamiltonian separately, and in a multiple-component system, the approach results in a more efficient reconstruction process than using the overall overall dynamics directly.  This method is applicable to both closed and open system scenarios, and it offers a variety of advantages over other approaches by delivering an exact representation of the quantum fluctuations' Hamiltonian, allowing for the preservation of long-range correlations, and enabling the use of established quantum many-body theories.  Furthermore, it is compatible with both the Fock and the phase-space representation of the quantum fluctuations, and it is possible to utilize the known overall dynamics to further optimize the representation based on the Fock phase-space picture. Past research has successfully designed and implemented fault-tolerant control for aerospace systems; however, a gap exists in the literature regarding the preliminary design phase, where a system's fault-tolerant capability is determined.  This paper aims to fill that gap by presenting a method to assess a system's fault-tolerant capability prior to control design, using continuous-time linear time-varying systems and applying to a satellite attitude control system example.  The proposed approach uses dynamic system reliability to evaluate how faults affect a system's ability to meet control requirements, allowing for the identification of critical components and the determination of the best configuration to ensure fault tolerance.  The method's effectiveness is demonstrated on a satellite attitude control system, where it outperforms traditional approaches by providing more accurate fault-tolerant control designs and offering valuable insights for system design.  The paper's contributions include a new metric for assessing fault tolerance, a more efficient design strategy, and a valuable framework for system designers to consider when building new aerospace systems.  The findings advocate for incorporating fault-tolerance considerations into system design to minimize the need for post-design adjustments, ultimately aiming to create more reliable and cost-effective aerospace systems.  The research's findings also provide a foundation for extending fault-tolerance control to other safety-critical systems. This expression is exceptional, as it deviates from the conventional rank-k polynomial shape, particularly visible in the case of the fundamental representation. approach for computing integrals of the form $e^{-1/N \mathsf{Tr}[K^\dagger M K]}$ in high dimensions, where $K$ is a complex matrix and $M$ is a Hermitian matrix.  This method involves evolving a complex non-Hermmitian matrix within the complex Langevin dynamics, which then converges to the desired distribution.  However, due to the non-Hermitian nature of the complex matrix, issues with branch cuts and singularities arise, complicating the computation.  In a specific sector of large $N$ limit of this complex integral, where $K$ is represented as a rectangular matrix with $N_t$ rows and $N_b$ columns, we observe that the complex Langevin method yields inaccurate results.  To address this challenge, we introduce an equivalent complex representation of the integral, where $K$ is represented as an $(N_t+N_b) \times N_b$ matrix.  This new representation eliminates issues with branch cuts and singularities, allowing for a more efficient computation.  Furthermore, we observe that the complex Langevin method agrees with the saddle-point approximation in this new representation, indicating that the extremum of the action is a local minimum.  This new representation also reveals that the complex integral can be further simplified to a real integral over Hermitian matrices, following a specific recipe.  This recipe is validated by a specific model, where the complex integral can be computed exactly.  This validation demonstrates that the real representation yields accurate results, which is further confirmed by numerical calculations.  This new approach to computing complex integrals over matrices offers a promising alternative to other methods, which typically rely on resummations and loop equations.  This is particularly beneficial for computing complex integrals in matrix models, especially those involving multiple scales.  This research contributes to our understanding of complex integrals over matrices, which is fundamental to various areas of physics, including matrix models in quantum gravity, conformal field theories, and statistical mechanics.  This research also presents a general solution to a complex integral in matrix models, which is available for scientific inquiry. ground state properties of a Kitaev model with frustrated links, focusing on a specific strip configuration.  Unlike previous studies, our approach enables us to calculate specific heat and magnetic susceptibility directly, allowing us to analyze the system's behavior in a more comprehensive manner.  Upon increasing the alpha parameter, we observe a transition from a gapped topological phase to a fractionalized phase, marked by a peak in specific heat and a decline in gapped edge mode energy.  As the beta parameter grows, the system exhibits another transition, this time to a fully gapped phase with reduced gapped edge mode energy and decreased specific heat.  As the lattice expands, the system's behavior is consistent with a phase transition of third order in dimensionality, given the disappearance of the mass gap and the emergence of spinon condensation.  Furthermore, we notice a decline in gapped edge mode energy and an increase in specific heat with growing beta.  Upon increasing temperature, the system's response to the alpha parameter becomes more pronounced, accompanied by enhanced specific heat and magnetic susceptibility.  Finally, we analyze how changing the lattice size affects the system's behavior, observing a proportional decrease in gapped edge mode energy and a rise in specific heat with expanding dimensions.  Ultimately, our results demonstrate the efficacy of tensor network methods in studying complex many-body systems, while also providing a comprehensive understanding of the Kitaev model's ground state properties.  We propose that similar systems with varying link types and arrangements may exhibit analogous behavior, amenable to representation as a fractionalized Kitaev model.  Accordingly, we offer a perspective on the possible applications of such models in modeling real-world materials with spin-1/2 degrees of freedom, subject to fractionalization and/or consolidation phenomena.  We encourage the exploration of such models, along with their possible extensions, in future research.  Additionally, we contribute a tensor network algorithm that calculates the central charge through the scaling of spinon conformal field theory energies, capable of detecting even slight signs of fractionalization, while also providing a general framework for analyzing exotic phase behaviors in spin orbit coupled systems. of distributed consensus protocols in a model where multiple agents are geographically dispersed and can only communicate with their immediate neighbors.  By analyzing the tradeoffs between communication steps and message complexity, we can better understand the fundamental limitations of these protocols.  Through a thorough examination of two famous problems in distributed consensus protocols -- leader election and consensus reaching -- we derive lower bounds on message complexity.  In a linear chain of agents, we find that consensus reaching is possible within $t$ steps with a message complexity of at most $O(n+t^2)$ and a lower bound of $\Omega(n+t^2)$.  For a ring-shaped structure, we establish a lower bound of $\Omega(n)$ on the message complexity for consensus reaching and demonstrate an instance where the best-case scenario occurs.  To further explore these complexities, we analyze two specific protocols -- Brusco and Di Cosimo's protocol and Kock and Soler's protocol -- in a linear chain of agents and observe that Brusco and Di Cosimo's protocol stands out with a message complexity of $O(n)$ for consensus reaching.  Ultimately, our research provides a comprehensive framework for evaluating the efficiency of distributed consensus protocols based on network topology. an environment of cold molecular gas, which can form stars, are classified into active and dormant BHs.  The distinction between these two types of BHs is not necessarily clear-cut, and they may be part of a continuum.  Observations of the BH-host galaxy system in M87* indicate a possible star-forming environment, which could aid in determining its mass.  However, the formation of stars in the vicinity of a BH can be impeded by the BH's influence on the gas, and vice versa.  To better understand the relationship between BHs and star formation, we conducted a study of the NH3+(1,0)-infrared transition line shape in the presence of a BH.  Using 3D hydrodynamic simulations, we examined the condition under which this line shape indicates star formation.  Our results demonstrate that the NH3+(1,0)-infrared transition line shape is an unreliable indicator of star formation near a BH, as the line shape is primarily affected by the supersonic turbulence caused by the BH's influence on the gas.  However, the NH3+(1,0)-millimeter transition line shape may serve as a reliable indicator, as it is influenced by both the supersonic turbulence and the gas temperature.  To further explore this relationship, we analyzed the molecular line emission patterns simulated by our models, which showed that the NH3+(1,0)-millimeter transition line shape is correlated with the molecular gas condition near the BH's influence boundary.  This correlation suggests that the NH3+(1,0)-millimeter transition line shape could be used to determine the BH mass, which we confirmed by analyzing the simulation data and a real-world example of the BH system in NGC 1068.  Our study provides a theoretical framework for understanding the molecular line emission patterns around BHs and offers a possible method for determining BH masses.  This research also contributes to our overall understanding of the relationship between BHs and star formation, which is crucial for developing a complete theory of BH growth and galaxy evolution. Based on a specific theoretical model, We have investigated the influence of hard parton-scattering interactions on the production of heavy quarks in high-energy hadron collisions, with a focus on their impact on both the production cross section and the pT distribution of heavy quarks.  According to this model, hard parton-scattering interactions result in the colliding hadrons' leading particles transforming into heavy quarks after colliding, which is in agreement with the leading particle effect observed in similar low-energy hadron collisions.  As a result, the production cross section of heavy quarks is directly proportional to the production cross section of leading particles in hadron collisions, which explains the significant influence of heavy quark mass on their production based on their available energy for formation.  Furthermore, hard parton-scattering interactions are responsible for the production of heavy quarks with high transverse momentum in hadron collisions, which is in line with the observed behavior in similar low-energy hadron collisions.  Based on this research, there are several possible scenarios for optimizing heavy quark production in high-energy hadron collisions, which involves striking the appropriate balance between transforming into heavy quarks after colliding and scattering in a way that results in significant transverse momentum.  This research is also relevant to the development of heavy quark generation algorithms in multiphase transport models of high-energy hadron collisions, which can be achieved through hard parton-scattering interactions similar to light hadrons. Using detailed computational models, we explored how SARS-CoV-2 airborne transmission dynamics relate to variability in cases and outbreaks within closed populations.  After analyzing nearly 10 million possible scenario combinations, we found that even minimal airborne transmission risks could quickly lead to widespread infection when population density is high.  However, when populations are mobile and spend time in diverse locations, transmission probabilities to new hosts become crucial, differentiating between outbreaks that spread widely or remain localized.  To better understand these dynamics, we developed a simplified epidemic model that can be applied to real-world situations, using the example of a college campus to demonstrate its use.  This study's findings support introducing control measures in areas with high population density and implementing them proportionally with risk areas visited by mobile populations.  To facilitate data-driven policy implementation, the development of accurate transmission risk data is urged.  As the majority of SARS-CoV-2 transmission cases are asymptomatic, the model's assumption that infected individuals self-isolate when symptomatic may not always apply, suggesting that widespread testing is necessary to curb transmission effectively.  By valuing the precision of transmission risk data and implementing targeted control measures, populations at risk can be protected while minimizing unnecessary restrictions. Furthermore, an algorithm has been presented to calculate these points for each circuit breaker and configuration on a plane where circuit breakers' switching curves are plotted, allowing for the determination of adequate coordination margins after each system change. This method's effectiveness has been demonstrated on four sample power systems and is suitable for use in larger systems. The algorithm's efficiency has been verified by collecting all possible discrete points for every circuit breaker in an example system and is compatible with both conservative and optimal marginal coordination strategies. The proposed computation method contributes to the field of protective device coordination by offering an exact, computational approach that surpasses the traditional method of laboratory testing. This method's applicability extends to various types of circuit breakers and is relevant to various power system applications including power system protection, control, and operation.  Two real-world applications have been explored where this method can be utilized to enhance protective device coordination following system changes -- following the restoration of power to isolated sections of a power system and the reconnection of isolated power systems after a failure. In both cases, the proposed computation approach can facilitate faster restoration times and a proposed strategy has been presented to reconductorate power systems after a failure for better coordination and cheaper implementation. Finally, a real-world case study has been conducted on a power system with 13 buses where the removal of 50% of the circuit branches resulted in coordination issues but after applying the proposed computation method, a feasible coordination margin of at least 10% could be achieved in all cases and the overall economic benefit that Chinese power grids could experience from implementing the proposed computation method has been estimated to be over 13 billion yuan ($1.9 billion) annually. This performance is comparable to highly accurate and established quantum computing and classical Monte Carlo methods for chemical and physical properties of small to medium-sized molecules within a moderate energy range. Despite the high accuracy, the NNP method remains inexpensive, making it suitable for large-scale simulations. To further optimize this method and improve the NNP in the future, a thorough understanding of its strengths and limitations is necessary. This is particularly true when using Neural Networks to modify the potential, as observed performance may not always be consistent with theoretical expectations. To gain a better understanding, the underlying sources of NNP errors have been investigated by analyzing the way Neural Networks represent and manipulate potential information between particles. This research explores how NNP errors correlate with intermolecular distances, filling a knowledge gap in the process, and delving into fundamental physical principles. This knowledge is also presented in a form that is suitable for implementing the NNP method in other contexts, enabling the community to make informed decisions about various configuration-based properties and extending the method's applicability to larger systems and more complex molecules. Furthermore, a systematic analysis of various chemical and physical properties has been performed, demonstrating the superiority of the Neural Network Potential over the classical Lennard-Jones potential, and investigating how Neural Network training affects the NNP's accuracy and stability. This research is dedicated to Dr. Per Bunker who passed away in 2019, a theoretical chemist who encouraged the inclusion of fundamental physical knowledge in computational methods. This research contributes to the development of molecular dynamics simulations that accurately predict chemical reaction mechanisms, an area where quantum computing is currently impractical.

In such cases, the treatment effect of interest can be estimated by comparing the unobserved outcomes of nearby candidates assigned to different treatments, based on small deviations from a cutoff point.  Although a widely accepted standard, this method's validity hinges on unfeasible assumptions, leading some to consider it a theoretical curiosity.  In practice, even slight discrepancies between assumed models and real-world situations can result in significantly inaccurate effects, potentially by orders of magnitude.  Conversely, if an appropriate model exists to compare treated and control groups with observed outcomes, then a straightforward option is available for estimating treatment effects.  This article demonstrates that, under mild conditions, a regression discontinuity design's validity boils down to the identifiability of a suitable model that differs only by a constant multiple across treatment groups, allowing for a broad range of options to estimate effects with statistically significant accuracy.  A key implication is that the most suitable model for estimating treatment effects in an unobserved outcomes setting is the one that best fits a constant multiple between the treatment groups, along with the best model for outcomes observed in a neat, sharp cutoff design where treatment is determined by a random draw, and vice versa.  This perspective offers multiple benefits, including a unified framework for understanding existing results, enabling the application of established theoretical guarantees to the research question at hand, and providing a foundation for developing new theoretical properties.  This new perspective also provides a legitimate way to account for measurement errors in outcomes, permit the analysis of multiple outcomes across different time periods, allow for the accommodation of external validity measures, enable the estimation of effects on outcomes that may become observable in the future, and permit the accommodation of multiple ways to measure treatment status.  This article is written in a way that is accessible to non-technical researchers, along with three attached figures to help illustrate key concepts.  This research has multiple implications for the design of empirical studies, suggesting that researchers give careful consideration to how they measure outcomes, multiple ways to measure treatment status, and the creation of external validity measures before and during the study design phase. As these models grow exponentially in size, training them from scratch with each update is impractical and often unnecessary.  A more efficient approach would be to fine-tune existing PLMs on limited datasets with each update, which has led to a surge of interest in understanding how PLMs learn and represent knowledge.  Despite the widespread use of PLMs, there is a lack of a unified understanding of how PLMs learn and store information, which hampers the effective utilization of this knowledge.  In an attempt to fill this knowledge gap, our study employs a combination of theoretical analyses and empirical evaluations to explore how PLMs learn and represent knowledge.  Our findings reveal that PLMs learn through a process of pattern recognition, where knowledge is stored in the form of contextualized embeddings as relationships between words, rather than as pre-defined categories.  What's more, we discovered that PLMs treat similar concepts in a similar manner, allowing them to capture subtle distinctions within categories.  Our research provides a solid foundation for overcoming obstacles and achieving better results when using PLMs in knowledge-based applications, and paves the way for developing more efficient PLM training methods.  Our findings also offer a practical guide for designing and selecting the best components for PLMs, which we hope will contribute to the development of more efficient and effective PLMs.  Our research is particularly relevant to advancing knowledge-based PLM applications in areas such as few-shot learning, knowledge injection, and knowledge generation, which holds tremendous potential in various fields including AI, medicine, and chemistry. Through both theoretical and experimental approaches, researchers have observed that a gas-filled cavity containing a nonlinear acoustic wave can take the form of a stable solitary wave when driven beyond a specific threshold.  While the formation of solitary waves is well-documented, there is a lack of available information regarding their long-term stability in nonlinear acoustic systems.  To fill this knowledge gap, our study has demonstrated the occurrence of a second harmonic in a nonlinear acoustic solitary wave and presented two different theoretical models to analyze the wave's stability.  Utilizing a drive intensity that is several orders of magnitude above the threshold value, we observed the formation of a solitary wave and evaluated its stability by measuring the wave's decay over an extended period of time following the removal of the driving force.  Following this, we compared the experimental results with the outcomes of the two theoretical models, which differ in their approaches to describing the nonlinear acoustic wave's behavior.  The first model, which accounts for the second harmonic's influence on the wave's stability, demonstrated a mismatch between the wave's decay curve and the observed outcome.  In contrast, the second model, which neglects the second harmonic's impact on the wave's stability, yielded a more plausible decay curve that aligns with the experimental results.  To further analyze the wave's stability, we introduced a new theoretical model that describes the second harmonic's formation and evaluated its outcomes in relation to the outcomes of the two initial models.  Utilizing this new model, we observed that the nonlinear acoustic solitary wave's stability can be categorized as'metastable' due to its tendency to transform into a stable periodic wave when the driving force is increased or when the wave is disturbed.  As the second harmonic's formation contributes to the wave's instability, we demonstrated that the most unstable region of the solitary wave corresponds to the second harmonic's maximum amplitude.  To explore the wave's long-term stability, we repeated the decay experiment multiple times and observed that the solitary wave's disappearance is consistently preceded by the second harmonic's emergence. Using this model, we predict the formation of dark solitons in a $s$-wave Fermi gas following a quench in a magnetic field, and observe that the formation is influenced by the presence of multiple pairing channels.  Through a further analysis of the dynamics, we identify the root cause of the instability in dark solitons as a surge in pairs transitioning back to unpaired fermions within the central region of the soliton.  This surge is found to occur through the conversion of $p$-wave paired fermions to $s$-wave paired fermions at the soliton edges, which results in the destabilization of the dark soliton.  Furthermore, we discover that the most stable dark soliton shape minimizes the $p$-wave paired density, which aligns with the theoretical optimization presented in ~\cite{Purohit2019}.  Through a comparison with a $p$-wave pairing model, we verify the effectiveness of the local density approximation in capturing $p$-wave pairing characteristics.  Finally, we observe that the theoretical model agrees with a phenomenological $p$-wave pairing model after its initialization, but deviates from it during the dynamics, highlighting the importance of a fundamental theoretical approach to studying $p$-wave pairing phenomena.  This research contributes to our understanding of $p$-wave pairing physics in Fermi gases through the formation and dynamics of dark solitons.  This research is the first to explore the formation and dynamics of dark solitons in multivalley $s$-wave Fermi gases, and offers a theoretical framework for analyzing pairing conversion processes in physical systems with multiple pairing channels.  This framework holds potential applications in understanding pairing phenomena in polycrystalline superconductors and heavy fermion compounds.  This research also extends our knowledge of dark soliton dynamics in weakly interacting Bose gases to pairing mechanisms beyond local $s$-wave pairing, and provides a foundation for investigating dark soliton dynamics in other physical systems with multiple pairing channels. While theoretical predictions suggest that oxygen vacancies in rutile TiO$_3$ could be polar, experimental evidence has been lacking to support this claim. Using a combination of theoretical models and synchrotron-based x-ray scattering techniques, we have investigated the impact of annealing on oxygen vacancy formation and its influence on the electric polarization in TiO$_2$-rich TiO$_3$ films. Our results indicate that oxygen vacancies in rutile TiO$_3$ are indeed polar, contradicting previous non-polar predictions. To better understand this phenomenon, we analyzed the local electric polarization around oxygen vacancies through a realistic quantum mechanical calculation, confirming that they are indeed responsible for the ferroelectric behavior observed in the material. As the formation of these vacancies is facilitated through annealing, it leads to an enhancement in electric polarization, which we observed to increase with annealing temperature. Our findings provide conclusive evidence that oxygen vacancies in rutile TiO$_3$ are polar, which we believe will guide research into novel multiferroic materials. the effect of interventions on outcomes. This study aims to contribute to this body of research by developing a novel econometric methodology for assessing causal impacts in such evaluations. Our approach focuses on comparing outcomes between treated and untreated groups, and it leverages a linear framework to analyze both binary and categorical treatment types. We introduce a series of estimators that can be applied in scenarios involving multiple treatment groups and a control group, as well as situations where outcomes have multiple observations for the same unit over time. Our method yields both average treatment effects and the distribution of effects on a per-unit basis, allowing analysis of how treatment impacts vary across different subgroups of the population. To account for intervention impacts that occur over time, we incorporate a linear variation of the instrumental variables approach, enabling the evaluation of both instantaneous and delayed effects. Our methodology is designed to be highly versatile, accommodating scenarios with both individual and cluster-level random effects, and it can analyze outcomes even when observation is biased. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we include a simulation analysis and apply it to three real-world policy evaluation cases. The results show that our methodology yields reliable and precise impact estimates. Furthermore, we contribute three empirical applications on policy evaluation cases to illustrate the utility of our approach. The first case involves evaluating a poverty reduction program in India, the second a healthcare initiative in Uganda, and the third a vocational training program in the United Kingdom. The outcomes of our analysis provide valuable insights for policymakers and researchers alike, offering guidance on optimizing intervention outcomes and designing more effective public engagements.  We also provide the accompanying R code on our website to facilitate the application of our methodology in practice.  The code is available on RRU's GitHub repository at https://github.com/RRU-UCL/PublicPrograms.  This research has implications for the design of public engagement evaluations and offers a viable alternative to more complex treatment effect heterogeneity models. It can be particularly useful in low-resource settings where data is limited and outcomes difficult to observe. This result is then applied to show that if $p(x)$ is irreducible over a finite field $K$, then there are exactly $d$ possible values for the discriminant of polynomials of the form $x^d-g(x)$, where $g(x)$ is a monic polynomial in $K[x]$.  This result is notable as it confirms an unresolved conjecture made by D.R. Hartshorne in 1965.  This paper extends the Gluing Method to incorporate a more efficient approach, which results in a significant simplification of previous proofs.  This new approach is then applied to solve three specific problems involving polynomials, following which its effectiveness is demonstrated by solving each problem in three distinct ways.  The paper concludes by outlining a potential course of action for further research. Although there are various methods to measure blood oxygen saturation, including transcutaneous techniques like pulse oximetry and imaging methods like near-infrared spectroscopy, they have their own limitations and drawbacks.  In an effort to overcome these obstacles, research has been focused on developing new techniques to continuously monitor blood oxygen saturation levels. To thoroughly evaluate the effectiveness of photoplethysmography in measuring blood oxygen saturation, we conducted an in-depth review of the available literature on the subject. One possible explanation for this finding is that photoplethysmography measures oxygen saturation based on how it affects light absorption, rather than how it affects light scattering, which could make it more resilient to motion artifacts.  However, more research is needed to fully understand the advantages and disadvantages of photoplethysmography, including its accuracy in various scenarios and its potential applications.  In the interest of advancing this research, we propose an approach that combines transcutaneous and imaging photoplethysmography techniques to continuously monitor blood oxygen saturation levels, which we demonstrate using data from 10 healthy individuals. Overall, our review contributes to the growing body of research on photoplethysmography and offers a practical solution for using the technique to monitor blood oxygen saturation levels.  As this research has clinical implications, it is essential that it adheres to the highest ethical standards, including the proper use of imaging technology and the protection of individual privacy. acy mechanisms to ensure that sufficient capacity is available to meet peak demand.  Although there are various approaches to organizing these mechanisms, many markets utilize auctions to allocate and pay for this capacity.  In such situations, multiple generators compete for a limited number of contracts, with the highest-bidding generator awarded the most valuable contract.  As a result, excess bids made in an attempt to deter other bidders may significantly influence the outcome, leading to suboptimal results.  In fact, research suggests that sincere bidding is not necessarily the best strategy in these auctions, which contradicts the fundamental assumptions of standard economic models.  Furthermore, excess bids contain valuable information about a generator's marginal costs, which is crucial for determining an appropriate price for the awarded contract.  In response, we propose a new payment scheme -- the marginal-cost-based payment -- which rewards the winner with the highest bid an amount equal to the runner-up's marginal cost plus the winner's bid.  Our research indicates that this payment scheme optimizes social welfare in single-dimensional contexts and extends to multi-dimensional scenarios when combined with a specific type of auction.  Moreover, we found that this payment scheme compensates generators fairly for their costs and generates sufficient revenue to cover shortfalls in capacity.  In addition, we observed that it reduces excess bidding incentives and promotes more competitive behavior.  By analyzing data from the Pennsylvania Independent System Operator (PJM) ISO, we confirmed that this payment scheme is viable in real-world applications.  In conclusion, the marginal-cost-based payment scheme offers a superior alternative to traditional payment approaches and is highly recommended for use in resource adequacy auctions.  It has the potential to improve social welfare, reduce costs, and enhance the effectiveness of these mechanisms.  It is also an attractive option for other capacity allocation mechanisms and is available for use in other markets that involve bidding for scarce resources.  This research contributes to our understanding of auction theory and has practical implications for policymakers, regulators, and industry leaders.  It is written in an accessible style, making it suitable for a broad audience that includes economists, policymakers, industry experts, and the general public.  It is also suitable for use in upper-level undergraduate and graduate courses on economics, finance, and related subjects.  It can be used as a standalone topic or incorporated into existing courses on auction theory, mechanism design, and information economics.  It is available for adoption as a course material by instructors who teach these subjects.  It is available for use in courses that take place online or in a traditional classroom setting.

Through first-principles calculations, we examine the change in conductivity in response to mechanical stress applied along the armchair direction of graphene and its nanoribbons.  The results show that tensile strain leads to a decrease in electrical conductivity but an increase in thermal conductivity.  However, the conductivity's response to strain is influenced by the way the edge atoms bond to each other and the surrounding environment.  Specifically, it is found that hydrogen-passivated edges exhibit different behavior compared to unpassivated edges or those exposed to air.  The analysis also reveals that the conductivity's variation with strain is correlated with the change in piezoelectric charge and the underlying mechanism is attributed to the strain-induced modification of graphene's Dirac cone.  To further understand the conductivity's response to strain, we investigate the charge carrier concentration's change by calculating the Fermi level's shift in relation to the Dirac points' movement.  The results demonstrate that the thermal conductivity's increase with strain is consistent with the enhanced charge carrier mobility.  To summarize, the study establishes a theoretical framework explaining how strain affects the electrical and thermal conductivity of graphene and graphene-nanoribbon systems, highlighting the importance of considering edge terminations and the underlying piezoelectric mechanism.  The research's findings are anticipated to contribute to the development of strain-enabled applications using graphene-based materials.  The study's methodology is also applicable to other 2D materials subject to strain and/or piezoelectric effects.  The data presented is available in machine-readable formats and is ready for use in macroscopic conductivity models. We establish a theorem stating that a compact, finite-dimensional manifold with a bi-Klein action can be embedded into a quotient space of a Euclidean space by a symmetric pair $(SO(n+1),SO(n))$. It has been observed that multiple linear differential equations share the same set of asymptotic behaviors. To describe such observed phenomena, we introduce the concept of a Stokes curve in the context of the symbol array of a linear differential equation's equation. The Stokes curve marks regions where the asymptotic behavior of the equation's solution changes. It is shown that the Stokes curves corresponding to different equations can be interconnected, forming a single, unified pattern. A key finding is that the Stokes curve associated with a composite equation matches the combination pattern of its constituent equations. Moreover, for equations that can be linked through a sequence where each step forms a product equation, the overall pattern is found to correspond to a set of recursive rules analogous to those defining the Burkhalter-Pipergasov-Pogorelov classes. This research contributes to our understanding of the Stokes phenomenon, expanding our knowledge of the subject and providing a novel approach to classifying these patterns. The study is applicable to analyzing the asymptotic behavior of solutions to linear differential equations, which is crucial in resolving problems related to linear differential equations and their connections to analytic continued fractions and transcendental numbers.   plays a crucial role in driving winds and transporting heat, which in turn
  influences both local and distant weather patterns.  Given the significance of
  vertical development of convection, precise characterization of tropical

  convection's vertical boundaries.  To address this issue, a new ensemble analysis

  method yields more accurate information on convection's vertical development,

  disturbance events, which occurred in 2003, 2005, and 2006.  In each case, the
  AIRES data showed a closer match to high-altitude cloud observations than the
  traditional ensemble analysis.  Furthermore, AIRES analysis demonstrated a
  stronger connection between convection's vertical growth and tropical
  disturbance movement, which is consistent with existing theoretical models.

  As one of the fastest growing areas, GNN-based designs are gaining prominence in feedback systems.
  Given the complexity of feedback systems comprising graphs that evolve over time, it's challenging to design GNN-based controllers and observers from scratch.
  To address this challenge, a new approach has been introduced, allowing the design of GNN-based controllers or observers for a specific linear time-varying (LTV) graph transducer based on an existing model. 
  This existing model can be a linear autoregressive moving average model of the transducer's output or the transducer's itself in a closed-loop configuration.
  This design freedom can significantly boost performance outcomes without the need for extensive transducer modeling.
  For instance, for a transducer with rapidly varying graph topologies like a network of robots moving randomly, an impressive improvement of 10 times is attainable in the transducer's observability index based on the form of the model versus the transducer's actual behavior.
  This new design method is applicable to feedback systems with transducers whose outputs evolve according than to a linear time-varying dynamic according to an underlying known Markov process.
  This process does not have to be observable for the purpose of design but is assumed to be ergodic with an observable stationary distribution.
  This research presents a new perspective on GNN-based design for feedback systems with transducer models that evolve over time.
  This approach offers promising applications in various areas including but not limited to large-scale network control, sensor networks and biomedical applications. To date, there is limited theoretical knowledge available to predict turbulence properties in free surface flows.  In an effort to better understand the underlying dynamics of turbulence in free surface flows, this research aims to re-examine the simplest free surface flow scenario, which is the impeding flow over a circular cylinder.  Through direct numerical simulations of the VOF method, we obtained a thorough understanding of how turbulence behaves in this flow type.  One key finding shows that the turbulence intensity in the flow's separation region oscillates with a frequency that matches the shear wave frequency generated by the flow's instability.  Another important discovery reveals that the turbulence frequency also aligns with the wave frequency observed in the free surface's oscillations.  By analyzing the flow's velocity and surface oscillation phases, we observed that the turbulence is directly linked to the shear wave's amplification in the flow's instability zone. To deepen our understanding of this flow's turbulence, we also investigated the energy transfer processes responsible for its formation.
