Although initial observations suggested possible signatures of physics beyond the Standard Model, more recent measurements have yielded similar results, contradicting this hypothesis.  To better understand these findings, we investigated the shape of non-identical pion correlations in proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV, with a focus on small transverse momentum ranges.  Our most precise results to date show no significant differences between identical and non-identical pion correlations.  To further analyze these correlations, we developed a new 3+1D hydrodynamic model that includes pion interaction information and tested it against existing data on identical pion correlations.  Following successful model verification, we employed the model to predict non-identical pion correlation shapes for various transverse momentum thresholds.  Our results indicate that non-conservation of pion species in local equilibrium is responsible for observable non-identical pion correlations, contradicting a previous theoretical prediction.  Our research provides compelling evidence that these correlations are primarily influenced by hadron interaction crosscriptions, which are crucial for both understanding existing data and developing new theoretical models.  Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that non-identical pion correlations offer a novel approach for determining reaction crossection values in local equilibrium scenarios.  We present preliminary reaction crossection estimates for pions and kaons, along with a proposal for a more comprehensive theoretical investigation.  Our findings contribute valuable insights for both heavy ion physics research and the study of little $x$ behavior in hadron collisions. mechanism called Adversarial Token Eraser (ATE), which effectively removes embedded adversarial noise by modifying tokens in neural network models.  Unlike typical defense strategies that focus on improving model robustness, ATE targets the source of embedded noise and eliminates it at its inception, thereby enhancing purity of input data and reducing the impact of noise on models.  Experimental results on TF-GAN and BigGAN models demonstrate that ATE successfully removes noise and improves classification accuracy in both single-adversarial and multiple-adversarial attacks.  Furthermore, our research reveals that ATE achieves better performance compared to existing defense mechanisms, and our proposed regularized token eraser variant (RTE) exceeds the best available method (Boundary Asymmetric Discriminant Embedding) by 20% in classification accuracy following multiple-adversarial attacks.  Moreover, our findings suggest that a significant portion of token embeddings contribute to noise removal, implying that noise elimination is often token-specific, and our analysis on TF-GAN models reveals a positive correlation between noise sensitivity and frequency of token occurrences in real images.  Finally, our research demonstrates that noise elimination through ATE leads to better performance on real-world image noise compared to existing strategies, which implies its potential applications in noise reduction across various real-image scenarios. Theoretical models predict that this hybrid material, dubbed "graphene-$λ$-BBDT-TTFA", exhibits zero resistance and pairs electrons at remarkably high temperatures of potentially up to 9.6 Kelvin.  To validate these predictions, we have synthesized the precursor molecule and incorporated it into the graphene structure through a molecular layer by layer growth process. The discovered superconducting pairs are anisotropic, consisting of electrons localized on adjacent molecules, which align parallel to each other within the hybrid material's lattice.  Theoretical modeling has shown that the repulsive interactions between electrons are mediated by molecular orbitals, which are highly susceptible to distortion, further supporting the observed anisotropic pairing behavior.  The discovery of anisotropic superconducting pairs in the graphene-$λ$-BBDT-TTFA hybrid material offers invaluable insights into unconventional superconductivity mechanisms, providing a novel model for research purposes. This event's X-ray and radio emissions began within a fraction of a second of each other, demonstrating a direct causal relationship between the two phenomena.  This discovery provides an opportunity to study these two phenomena simultaneously, allowing for a more comprehensive understanding of their characteristics and possible origins.  This data reveals that the X-ray and radio emissions from FRB 200219B/X are correlated, suggesting that they result from the same burst of energy released during a cataclysmic astrophysical event.  This event's large energy release and the presence of a host galaxy with normal intergalactic medium properties eliminate several theoretical explanations, but it is consistent with the "Central Engine" model, in which Fast Radio Bursts are caused by the collapse of a neutron star in a binary system, leading to a burst of energy that heats and accelerates magnetic field particles, resulting in both radio and X-ray emissions.  This discovery also provides evidence for the existence of a population of binary systems that contain neutron stars and emit Fast Radio Bursts, which are dispersed and detected as Fast X-ray Transients. beyond the Standard Model through particle collisions
  are being explored, including searches for mono-jet events accompanied by missing transverse momentum
  and searches for resonance production in like-sign dilepton events.  A more in-depth look at these
  search methodologies reveals their dependence on accurate theoretical predictions, particularly
  for background processes like $Z/Z'$ boson production in association with hadrons (vector boson
  associated production).  To ensure the effectiveness of these searches in detecting New Physics,
  it is imperative that these predictions are precise.  In the case of theoretical calculations for
  $Z/Z'$ associated production, this means eliminating errors associated with hadron colliders
  and/or the underlying particle model.  In the context of the Standard Model itself, this means
  achieving a precision of at least 1% to 2% for relevant $Z/Z'$ associated production processes
  to match the accuracy of missing transvergence momentum searches.  While leading-order (LO)
  perturbative quantum field theory is insufficient in achieving this precision, the combination
  of next-to-leading-order (NLO) perturbative quantum field theory and state-of-the-art resumination
  techniques is promising in meeting or even exceeding the required precision for these searches. 
  This thesis contributes to these efforts by exploring NLO perturbative quantum field theory
  matching issues in $Z/Z'$ associated production through a hadron's most significant particle component
  (the sea quark or antiquark).  In the case of $Z$ boson production in association with a quark
  and an antiquark ($\bar{q}q$), this research examines NLO matching problems related to the replacement
  of collinear quark and antiquark masses with their respective scale-dependent running quantities. 
  A novel approach is presented in resolving these matching issues by redefining NLO perturbative quantum
  field theory vertices and counterterms to eliminate collinear singularities.  This research also
  explores NLO matching issues related to the replacement of $Z'$ boson mass with its scale-dependent
  running quantity in $Z'$ boson production in association with a quark and an antiquark ($\bar{q}q$)
  through the renormalization group equation.  An effective field theory is introduced to resolve these
  matching issues by redefining NLO perturbative quantum field theory vertices and counterterms to
  eliminate infrared singularities.

Using a highly sensitive magnetometer, we have analyzed how local gravity field fluctuations influence magnetic field stability in ULALP detector experiments.  Our findings reveal that local gravity field fluctuations are not a significant source of magnetic field instability in ULALP detector experiments, as they result in negligible curvature variations on laboratory scales.   This proof stands out from the classical proofs that rely heavily on measure theory,
